title: Smallest Window Covering a Word
statement:
Given two strings s and t, find the shortest contiguous piece of s that contains every character of t, counting repeats: if t has two "a"s, the piece needs at least two "a"s. Other characters may appear in the piece too, and order does not matter.

Characters are case-sensitive: "a" and "A" are different.

Return that piece. If several pieces share the shortest length, return the leftmost one (the one that starts first). If no piece works, return the empty string "".

examples.why: "CAB" and "BAC" both have length 3. "CAB" starts first.
The piece needs two "a"s. A single "a" would cover the set of letters but not the count.
s has only one Q, so no piece can cover t.

constraints: s and t hold English letters (upper and lower case)
hints: For a fixed right end, which left ends give a valid piece? If [i, j] is valid, is [i − 1, j] valid too?
Grow the window on the right until it covers t. Then shrink it from the left as long as it stays valid; each such window is a candidate.
Keep a count of what t still needs and a single number 'missing' = how many characters of t, with repeats, are not yet in the window. The window is valid exactly when missing is 0.

explain.intuition:
If a window covers t, any wider window covers it too. So for each right end there is a smallest valid window, and as the right end moves right, its best left end never moves left. That is the sliding-window shape: the right edge expands until the window is valid, the left edge contracts while it stays valid, and both only move forward.

Checking "is it valid?" by comparing all counts every step would be slow. Instead keep need[c] (how many more of c the window must contain; it goes negative when there are extras) and missing, the total still owed. missing drops only when a character fills a real need and rises only when removing a character creates one. Record a window only when it is strictly shorter than the best so far; windows are met in left-to-right order, so the first one of the minimum length is the leftmost.
steps: Count the characters of t into need. Set missing = t.length, start = 0.
For each end: if need[s[end]] > 0, decrease missing. Then decrease need[s[end]].

While missing === 0: if the window [start, end] is strictly shorter than the best, record it. Then give back s[start]: increase its need, and if it becomes positive, increase missing. Move start right.
After the loop, return the recorded window, or "" if none was found.
pitfalls: Tracking a set of characters instead of counts. With t = "aa", one "a" is not enough.
Updating the best window with ≤. On a tie that replaces the leftmost answer with a later one.
Decreasing missing for every character of t that enters, even extras. Extras push need below 0 and must not count as filling a need.

complexity.space: O(k), k = distinct characters in t

solutions.title: Every start, extend until covered
solutions.idea: For each start, extend right until the window covers t, then compare its length with the best. Correct, but each start rescans the string.

solutions.title: Expand right, shrink left, with a missing counter
solutions.idea: Grow the window until it covers t, then shrink it from the left while it still does. A single counter tells whether the window is valid.

followups: t is tiny and s is huge but mostly made of characters not in t. How could you skip them quickly?
Return the rightmost window on ties instead. Which single comparison changes?
